Article Title: MAGA piles on to Morocco as Trump twits Spain over Ceuta
Article Text:
TOI correspondent from Washington:

The dramatic migrant surge into the Spanish North African enclave of Ceuta is quickly evolving from a humanitarian and border-security emergency into a geopolitical flashpoint, triggering President Trump, energizing the MAGA movement, and causing an explosion of online conspiracy theories linking the crisis to wider disputes over Iran, Gaza, and Nato.The MAGA boss on Friday used the events in Ceuta to reinforce one of the defining themes of his presidency -- that strong border enforcement is the ultimate measure of national sovereignty. While the White House stopped short of endorsing Morocco's longstanding territorial claim over Ceuta, Trump argued that the crisis demonstrated the consequences of weak immigration policies and inadequate border controls."It’s terrible. Remember that picture. That’s going to be us in three years if the wrong side gets in," Trump told Fox News on Friday, adding, "If the Democrats get in, you will not live a very good life." In a social media post reposting a video of the migrants breaching Ceuta, Trump’s immigration policy architect Stephen Miller wrote, "Democrats did this to America every single day for 4 years under Biden and they will do it again instantaneously, but orders of magnitude greater, if they are given any form of national power.The administration's messaging was amplified by the US Department of Homeland Security, whose official social media account declared: "If Spain had their own President Trump, this wouldn't be an issue. Citizens of Spain should take that into consideration." The remarks constituted a direct intervention in the domestic politics of a Nato ally and reflected the administration's effort to present Trump's immigration policies which many critics say is based on paranoia and exaggeration, as a model for Western governments.Within the broader MAGA ecosystem, the images from Ceuta were framed in even starker civilizational terms. Prominent conservative commentators described the episode as an "African invasion of Europe," arguing that uncontrolled migration threatened Europe's cultural identity and border integrity. Elon Musk, who has frequently warned that large-scale illegal immigration could transform Western societies, was among influential figures highlighting the Ceuta images as evidence of what they view as Europe's failure to secure its frontiers.The crisis has also unfolded against an increasingly strained US-Spain relations, including Madrid's refusal to support American military operations against Iran, its opposition to Israeli military actions in Gaza, its recognition of a Palestinian state, and persistent disputes with the Trump administration over Nato defense spending. Trump has repeatedly criticized Spain as failing to meet alliance obligations while questioning Madrid's reliability as a strategic partner.Those tensions have fueled a parallel narrative, with numerous social media posts claiming Morocco deliberately relaxed border controls with encouragement from Washington and Israel in order to punish Spain for opposing US and Israeli policies. Some posts point to American security assistance for Morocco, expanding Israeli-Moroccan defense cooperation following the Abraham Accords, and reports that some US officials have examined shifting military assets from Spain to Morocco. Others cite opinion articles advocating stronger US support for Morocco's claims over Ceuta and Melilla.Ceuta occupies a uniquely sensitive geopolitical position. It was home to roughly 80,000 residents before the latest influx, and sits on Africa's Mediterranean coast opposite mainland Spain, attached to Morocco. Together with Melilla, it represents Spain's only land border with Africa. Although administered by Spain for centuries and regarded by Madrid as an integral part of the country, Morocco continues to claim both enclaves as occupied territory.The enclave's strategic importance extends far beyond migration. Located near the Strait of Gibraltar -- the narrow maritime passage connecting the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean -- Ceuta overlooks one of the world's busiest shipping corridors, through which roughly a tenth of global maritime trade passes. Like with Hormuz and the Gulf, control and security of the surrounding waters carry major military and commercial significance for Nato, Europe, North Africa and international energy supplies.
Article Summary: The dramatic migrant surge into the Spanish North African enclave of Ceuta is quickly evolving from a humanitarian and border-security emergency into a geopolitical flashpoint. The crisis has triggered President Trump, energizing the MAGA movement, and causing an explosion of online conspiracy theories linking the crisis to wider disputes over Iran, Gaza, and Nato.

Article Title: 'Remember that picture': Trump uses Ceuta crisis as warning for US voters
Article Text:
US Republicans frame the Cueta crisis narrative for upcoming elections

US President Donald Trump and his vice president JD Vance led far-right efforts on both sides of the Atlantic to exploit Spain's migration crisis, portraying the surge in Ceuta as a preview for America if Democrats regain power."It's terrible. Remember that picture. That's going to be us in three years if the wrong side gets in," Trump said in remarks quoted by Fox News. "If the Democrats get in, you will not live a very good life."The US president's comments come as his poll numbers have dropped into the low 30 percent range, with Democrats hoping to win at least partial control of Congress in the November midterm elections. The Ceuta crisis offers Republicans a chance to return to one of their signature political issues.Vance posted news footage of migrants pouring into Ceuta on X, writing that it highlighted "radical left-wing globalist policies that have enabled the Invasion of the West."White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller also weighed in, posting a video and claiming "Democrats will see your home trampled and stolen by invaders and they will rejoice."News footage of migrants overwhelming barriers to enter Ceuta, a tiny Spanish territory on the Moroccan coast, went viral across right-wing, Trump-allied social media accounts.In Europe, far-right leaders also seized on the crisis. Alternative for Germany co-leader Alice Weidel claimed in an X post that "Ceuta was left in ruins overnight" by the mass influx. She argued Germany is "likely the destination for most of these migrants" and called for securing borders and rigorously enforcing rejections.Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and the populist ruling coalition in Finland called for excluding Spain from the European visa-free zone. Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis, a Trump supporter, blamed Spain's policy of offering legal status to hundreds of thousands of migrants already in the country, saying "They are replacing Spaniards with migrants."Trump's 2024 election victory was fueled by voter concerns over migration on the US-Mexico border and his warnings of migrants committing crimes.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump and his vice president JD Vance led far-right efforts on both sides of the Atlantic to exploit Spain's migration crisis. News footage of migrants overwhelming barriers to enter Ceuta, a tiny Spanish territory on the Moroccan coast, went viral across right-wing social media accounts.

Article Title: A $215,280 Colorado home is being sold without inspections; the buyer must remove the woman living inside, and she says she will not leave
Article Text:
Viral Colorado home listing warns buyers they must remove the ‘occupant’ living inside

A 15-year foreclosure dispute

Occupant plans to fight eviction

A home listed for $215,280 in Colorado has gone viral after people noticed an unusual Zillow listing that bans home inspections and leaves the buyer responsible for evicting the current resident. The woman living in the house says she has no intention of leaving.The three-bedroom, two-bathroom home is located in Nunn, a small town about 25 miles from Fort Collins. The listing gained widespread attention after the social media account Zillow Gone Wild shared screenshots of it on X, formerly Twitter, where it received more than four million views.The listing clearly states that the house is being sold with someone still living inside. Buyers are not allowed to enter the property or carry out inspections before purchasing it. It also says the listing agent has never been inside the home and that the buyer will be fully responsible for taking legal possession of the property after the sale."The ad is unbelievable, right?" current resident Tori McMechan told local station 9News. "Who would buy a house without seeing it while someone is still living there?"Behind the viral listing is a long legal fight over foreclosure, mortgage ownership, and family tragedy.McMechan moved into the home in 2006 with her husband, James McMechan, who had bought the property four years earlier. James died in a car crash in 2010, making the home especially meaningful to McMechan because it was where they raised their children and one of the last major purchases her husband made before his death.According to the Greeley Tribune, James McMechan died in a single-vehicle crash shortly after police said he threatened several members of the Nunn town board with a knife. Around the same time, Tori McMechan lost her job as the town's clerk and treasurer."This is the last thing my husband bought for me before he passed away," McMechan told 9News. "This is where I raised my children."Financial problems began in June 2010 when the mortgage went into default. Weld County court records show the property has faced at least six foreclosure cases over the past 15 years. McMechan said that after her husband's death, she tried to continue making mortgage payments, but loan servicers refused to accept them because the mortgage was only in her husband's name.Over the years, the mortgage was transferred between several financial companies before ending up with Deutsche Bank National Trust Company."We took out the loan on this house in 2006," McMechan told 9News. "By 2021, the house would have been completely paid off."McMechan later filed two lawsuits claiming it was unclear who legally owned the mortgage because it had been transferred several times. Both cases were dismissed. Last year, the Colorado Court of Appeals ruled that even if her claims were true, they were not enough to stop the foreclosure.The listing agent told 9News that despite handling thousands of foreclosed homes during his career, he had never listed a property that was still occupied.Real estate experts say buying an occupied foreclosure carries major legal and financial risks. In most home sales, the seller delivers the property vacant. In this case, ownership of the house transfers to the buyer, but the resident does not have to leave immediately. The new owner would have to go to court and file an eviction case to remove the occupant legally.Eviction proceedings can take months and cost thousands of dollars in legal expenses. Buyers also take on the risk of purchasing a home they have never seen, meaning they could face hidden structural problems, maintenance issues, or unpaid local charges.McMechan believes she still has legal options. She pointed to an October 2024 Colorado Supreme Court ruling that allows tenants, in certain situations, to request a jury trial during eviction proceedings. Such a request could delay an eviction for months or even years.Banks often sell foreclosed properties "as-is" and without inspections to avoid the time and expense of removing occupants themselves. By listing the Nunn home well below typical prices in Northern Colorado, the bank is effectively leaving those legal risks to the buyer.No matter who eventually buys the property, McMechan says she plans to stay and continue fighting to keep her home."I'm staying," McMechan told 9News. "They can come on in, but I'm not leaving."
Article Summary: The three-bedroom, two-bathroom home is located in Nunn, a small town about 25 miles from Fort Collins. The listing clearly states that the house is being sold with someone still living inside. Buyers are not allowed to enter the property or carry out inspections.

Article Title: What happened to 'Green Cards stapled to diplomas': Attorney reacts to proposal of $100,000 OPT fee
Article Text:
US wants to impose a $100,000 fee on OPT.

What is OPT? Why is this a new target of the Donald Trump administration?

During the presidential campaign before the 2024 election, Donald Trump said he would staple a Green Card to the diplomas so that foreign students could stay in the US and work after finishing their education. It has been a long way since that time, and now that the administration is proposing a $100K fee for Optional Practical Training, the distance between what Trump had promised and what his administration is doing or planning to do has never been greater.“What I want to do, and what I will do, is — you graduate from a college, I think you should get automatically, as part of your diploma, a green card to be able to stay in this country,” Trump had said during an interview with “The All-In Podcast" in June 2024.Experts said if the administration imposes a $100K fee on OPT, foreign students will not choose US schools and universities. "The ability to work for a year after graduation is a major reason students pick US schools. It allows them to get real US work experience that will look good on their resume wherever they end up building their career," attorney Adrian Pandev said."F-1 OPT is also the only immigration status in which a young entrepreneur can launch a company in their field of study without having to invest significant capital or meet other difficult requirements.It gives a student 1 year to build something truly meaningful. I have seen so many great companies start this way. We sure have come a long way from 'green cards stapled to diplomas'..." Pandev said.OPT is the Optional Practical Training program, which allows international students on an F-1 visa to work legally in their field of study. After their degree, they can stay in the US legally and work for 12 months under this program. This program does not have a fee to pay to the government as of now.But recently, several Republican leaders raised alarms over how the OPT became a pipeline for the H-1B. Companies hire OPT students as trainees and then file for their H-1B visa, shutting Americans out of this exclusive process teeming with foreigners.The Donald Trump administration earlier imposed a $100,000 fee on H-1B visas, but it was stayed by a court order. Now the administration is planning to bring the $100K fee to OPT programs. The administration has already imposed a four-year validity to F-1 visas afte which the students have to file for a renewal, extension.
Article Summary: US wants to impose a $100,000 fee on Optional Practical Training. Donald Trump said he would staple a Green Card to the diplomas so that foreign students could stay in the US and work after finishing their education. The administration has already imposed a four-year validity to F-1 visas afte which the students have to file for a renewal.

Article Title: US proposes stricter J-1 visa compliance rules; Indian researchers, doctors could be affected
Article Text: Thousands of Indian researchers, doctors, professors and trainees heading to the US on J-1 exchange visitor visas could face stricter compliance requirements under a proposal by the Trump administration to tighten oversight of one of America's most widely used academic and cultural exchange programmes.This proposal by the US Department of State (DOS) comes just weeks after the Trump administration finalised a separate rule ending the decades-old ‘duration of status’ visa system for J-1 exchange visitors and replacing it with fixed admission periods of up to four years, requiring many participants to seek visa extensions if their exchange programmes continue beyond that period.Now, DOS has published a proposed rule that would significantly revise how exchange visitors maintain their status, expand the grounds on which participation in the programme may be terminated, formally establish procedures for reinstating those who fall out of status, and impose additional compliance responsibilities on programme sponsors. The proposal has been published in the Federal Register and is open for public comment for sixty days before it is finalised.Unlike the H-1B, which is an employment visa, the J-1 visa is intended to promote educational and cultural exchange. A little over 12,000 J-1 visas were issued to Indian nationals in fiscal 2024, it is widely used by Indian postdoctoral researchers, scientists, university professors, medical professionals undergoing residency or fellowship training, teachers, interns and trainees participating in programmes sponsored by US universities, research institutions and teaching hospitals.While the proposal does not alter eligibility requirements for obtaining a J-1 visa or create new visa categories, it raises the importance of maintaining compliance throughout the period of exchange.A key feature of the proposal is the introduction of a comprehensive definition of what constitutes a ‘failure to maintain exchange visitor status’. At present, the requirements governing an exchange visitor's status are spread across different provisions of the regulations. The proposed rule consolidates the status-maintenance requirements into a single framework, clearly setting out when an exchange visitor may fall out of status, including through unauthorised employment, failure to meet programme requirements or overstaying the authorised programme period.The proposal also broadens and clarifies the grounds on which the DOS may terminate an individual's participation in the Exchange Visitor Program. In addition to violations of programme requirements, the proposed rule identifies grounds such as specified criminal conduct, fraud or misrepresentation, national security-related concerns and other circumstances that render an exchange visitor ineligible to continue participating in the programme. DOS said the changes are intended to strengthen programme integrity, improve oversight and ensure that exchange visitors continue to meet eligibility requirements throughout their stay in the US.Another important aspect of the proposal is that it formally codifies the reinstatement process for exchange visitors who have fallen out of status. Although reinstatement has long been available through administrative practice, the proposed regulations would, for the first time, set out detailed eligibility criteria, documentation requirements and procedures for seeking restoration of status, providing greater transparency and consistency in how such requests are handled.The draft rule would also place additional responsibilities on designated programme sponsors, including universities, research institutions and teaching hospitals. Sponsors would be required to monitor participants more closely, promptly report events affecting an exchange visitor's eligibility and maintain accurate records in the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS)."The proposal would also establish a formal process allowing exchange visitors to challenge programme termination decisions, while requiring sponsors to terminate participants who provide false or incomplete information during the application process or while participating in the programme.
Article Summary: US Department of State has published a proposal to tighten oversight of one of America's most widely used academic and cultural exchange programmes. A little over 12,000 J-1 visas were issued to Indian nationals in fiscal 2024. It is widely used by Indian postdoctoral researchers, scientists, university professors, medical professionals undergoing residency or fellowship training.

Article Title: A Michigan woman owns 19 acres between two planned Toll Brothers communities; she is suing over her only access route and a proposed wastewater discharge
Article Text:
Toll Brothers sued by owner of land surrounded by 107-luxury home project

Fight over property access

Developers reject the claims

Long history of the development

Why easement disputes matter

A Michigan woman who owns 19 acres of wooded land between two planned luxury housing developments has filed a lawsuit against homebuilder Toll Brothers. The dispute centers on her property access rights and plans to build a private wastewater treatment facility near her land, reports MLive.Susan Miller filed the lawsuit in Washtenaw County Trial Court against Toll Brothers Inc., its subsidiary Toll Northeast V Corp, and former developer Red Equities LLC. Her undeveloped property in Lodi Township lies between the planned Arbor Preserve-North and Arbor Preserve-South communities, where developers want to build 107 luxury homes along with two private wastewater treatment plants.According to court documents, Miller says the developers ignored her property rights and local environmental rules. She claims detention ponds and one of the treatment plants will release treated wastewater just 10 feet from her property line, changing the natural flow of water into a creek on her land that connects to the Rouse Drain and the Saline River."Toll's plan for a large luxury housing development claims to address housing needs, but instead destroys a natural landscape and ignores Lodi Township's environmental protections," Miller said in a statement.Her attorney, Sam Estenson, said the developers have "surrounded and besieged" Miller after she refused to sell her land."At meeting after meeting, local residents raised concerns about environmental damage and violations of township rules, but Toll showed little interest in those concerns," Miller added.One of the main issues in the lawsuit is the only road that provides access to Miller's property from Waters Road.According to the lawsuit, Miller signed a conditional agreement with Red Equities in 2021 to end her original private road easement in exchange for a new access road through Arbor Preserve-South. The agreement required the new road to be completed by December 31, 2025. If it was not built by then, the agreement would automatically expire.Miller says that although the new road was never built, the developers recorded both the termination of her original easement and the replacement access agreement with the Washtenaw County Register of Deeds in 2023 without informing her.Estenson said the developers pressured Miller by warning that she could be forced to pay more than $1 million toward the cost of building an access road if her original easement remained in place.Miller is asking the court to restore her original access easement, cancel the recorded replacement agreement, and overturn the final site plan approved by Lodi Township officials.She is also seeking more than $25,000 in damages, along with legal fees and court costs.Toll Brothers declined to comment directly on the lawsuit because the case is still before the court.In court filings, the defense denied the allegations, calling the lawsuit a "frivolous attempt" to delay the Arbor Preserve project and cause financial harm to Toll Northeast.Alan Greene, a lawyer representing Toll Brothers, argued that Toll Brothers Inc. does not legally own the property. He said Toll Northeast V Corp is a separate company that owns the land and signed the local development agreements.The defense has asked the court to remove Toll Brothers Inc. from the lawsuit. It also argues that Miller's claims about the easement should be dismissed because they were filed after the legal time limit had expired.The development plans are linked to a court-approved agreement dating back to 2007. At that time, the previous developer, Peters-Summit LLC, sued Lodi Township after officials rejected an earlier proposal for the site.Although township zoning rules normally ban private wastewater treatment plants, the 2007 court agreement created an exception allowing them on this property.In 2020, Red Equities proposed building more than 400 multi-family housing units. After residents objected to the high density, the company revised the plan in 2023, reducing it to 107 single-family homes. The court agreement was then amended to match the new proposal.Toll Northeast V Corp bought the property in 2024 to move forward with the updated development.Estenson said Miller wants to keep her land in its natural state and hopes to donate it in the future for environmental conservation.Washtenaw County Trial Court Judge Julia Owdziej is expected to hear Miller's request for a preliminary injunction on Wednesday, August 5. A separate hearing on Toll Brothers' request to partially dismiss the lawsuit is scheduled for Wednesday, September 16.Property access disputes often become some of the most complicated issues in land development because an easement can determine whether land remains usable. In many cases, a property owner may legally own land but still depend on an easement across a neighboring parcel to reach a public road. If that access is restricted or replaced, the property's value and future use can be significantly affected. Courts generally examine the exact wording of easement agreements, whether any replacement access provides the same practical benefits, and whether all legal procedures were properly followed when changes were recorded.The Arbor Preserve project has drawn attention beyond Miller's lawsuit because it has faced years of public debate over environmental impacts, wastewater management, and compliance with local planning rules. Earlier versions of the proposal called for more than 400 housing units before the project was redesigned into a 107-home development. Even after those changes, residents continued raising concerns about water resources, private wastewater treatment plants, and the long-term effects on nearby properties during public meetings.
Article Summary: Susan Miller owns 19 acres of land between two planned luxury housing developments. Miller says developers ignored her property rights and local environmental rules. Miller is seeking more than $25,000 in damages, along with legal fees and court costs. Toll Brothers calls the lawsuit a "frivolous attempt" to delay the Arbor Preserve project.

Article Title: Travel alert for visa holders in US: Immigration experts say domestic flying has become risky, alarming rise in number of airport arrests
Article Text:
Immigration experts advise visa holders to cancel domestic travel plans amid what they called an alarming rise in the number of airport arrests.

What is happening? Who are getting arrested at airports?

'Avoid domestic air travel unless absolutely necessary'

If you are not in valid immigration status now...

Immigration experts warned against international travel for visa holders for the time being, as several instances of foreigners denied re-entry were reported. But now, the experts are urging people to exercise caution even for domestic travel because several cases of detainment have been reported in California, Colorado, Florida, Illinois, Kansas, Michigan, New Jersey, Texas, and Virginia.People with expired visas are at risk of getting detained at the airports. Generally, documents proving that your visa has expired but you already applied for an adjustment of status, or extension, or asylum would have allowed such people to remain in the US legally. But attorneys reported an alarming rise in airport arrests. Immigration attorney Rajiv Khanna said some of these detained people do not have criminal records; they have work authorization or advanced parole documents. Khanna said such individuals should speak with their lawyers, carry all important documents and be prepared for unreasonable delays.Business immigration attorney Lucy Magardichian said she recommends avoiding domestic air travel completely unless it's absolutely necessary. "We are seeing increased immigration enforcement activity at domestic airports, including reports of ICE arrests involving individuals whose underlying status has expired—even when a lawful extension or change of status is pending," she said.A pending EOS/COS does not necessarily protect you from immigration enforcement or arrest, she added.Immigration attorney Tsui H Yee said she advised her clients to cancel their vacation next week at the risk of sounding like an alarmist, but it's not worth the risk, she said. "In the past, I never had to worry about clients being nabbed by ICE for flying domestically. If someone had an outstanding deportation order or an administrative warrant, then that's a different story," she said."But in the last 2 weeks, there have been numerous reports of clients who had pending immigration applications being detained before or after landing on domestic flights.""The bottom line is that if you are not in valid immigration status now, you should avoid flying. For example, even if you filed an I-485 adjustment application before your nonimmigrant status expired, you could still be flagged as an enforcement priority," Yee said.
Article Summary: People with expired visas are at risk of getting detained at the airports. Some of these detained people do not have criminal records; they have work authorization or advanced parole documents. If you are not in valid immigration status now, you should avoid flying.

Article Title: Meet Kai Sato: The California sailor who spent 34 days lost at sea after his Hawaii dream turned into a fight for survival
Article Text:
PC: AI Generated

Solo sailor's Pacific Ocean voyage to Hawaii turned into a survival ordeal



When returning home was no longer possible



Repairing the boat with ordinary items



How he found food and fresh water



The mental struggle of surviving alone in the open ocean



For weeks, a small sailing boat drifted across a vast stretch of the Pacific with little certainty about where it would end up. Its lone occupant, 39-year-old Kai Sato from California, had set out hoping to complete his first solo voyage to Hawaii, but the journey quickly became something very different. Far from shipping routes and with limited supplies, he was forced to abandon the idea of simply reaching his destination and instead focus on getting through each passing day while carefully managing food, collecting rainwater whenever possible and conserving the limited resources still available aboard. By the time another vessel finally appeared on the horizon, more than a month had passed since his plans had fallen apart, leaving behind a story shaped less by adventure than by persistence and improvisation.According to Hawaii News, Sato left California's Catalina Islands on 7 June, beginning what he intended to be his first solo crossing of the Pacific to Hawaii. The trip had personal meaning. Years earlier, he had travelled the same route alongside an uncle, an experience that had stayed with him and encouraged him to attempt the crossing on his own.Only a couple of weeks into the voyage, everything changed. The sailboat's mast failed, removing the vessel's main source of power and leaving it at the mercy of wind and ocean currents.The route he had carefully planned disappeared almost immediately as the damaged boat drifted farther from where he wanted to be.The days immediately after the accident proved just as demanding emotionally as they were physically. Sato later described feeling overwhelmed by the situation, admitting that he struggled to see a way out during the first week after the damage occurred.He attempted to rely on the boat's engine to head back towards land, but that option soon disappeared when the fuel ran out. Without wind propulsion or enough fuel to motor home, the boat simply continued drifting, carried by currents moving him farther south instead of towards safety.After several days of uncertainty, he decided he needed to work with whatever equipment remained on board rather than wait for rescue.The damaged sailboat could not be restored properly at sea, but Sato managed to improvise a temporary solution using ordinary items he had onboard. PVC pipes and kayak paddles became makeshift replacements that allowed him to create a basic sailing system capable of giving him at least some control over the vessel.The repairs were far from ideal, yet they gradually helped him steer back towards one of the busy shipping corridors linking California and Hawaii. Reaching that area took weeks rather than days, but returning to a route travelled by commercial vessels offered the first realistic chance of being spotted.As the voyage dragged on, supplies became an even greater concern. His drinking water eventually ran out during July, forcing him to experiment with ways of collecting small amounts of fresh moisture.He filled containers with seawater and covered them using plastic bags, allowing condensation to form inside. The tiny amounts of fresh water produced by this process became an important source of hydration.Food remained scarce as well. Oatmeal lasted longer than expected because it was carefully rationed, while fish and squid that ended up on the boat added occasional meals that helped extend his supplies.Long periods alone at sea can become mentally exhausting, particularly when there is no clear idea of when help might arrive. Sato said he spent much of his time talking aloud, meditating and reflecting while surrounded only by open water.He also found comfort in memories of his uncle, whose earlier Pacific voyage had inspired his own attempt. Remembering that shared experience gave him something familiar to hold onto while facing long days without contact with other people.After weeks without seeing another vessel close enough to reach, Sato eventually spotted a ship operated by Pasha Hawaii. Even then, getting aboard was not immediate. Crew members needed more than one attempt before successfully lowering a rope ladder that he could climb safely.Once aboard, the contrast was immediate. Fresh water, fruit, clean clothes and a private cabin replaced the difficult conditions he had endured for weeks. Sato later described the moment as one of overwhelming relief after spending so long uncertain whether anyone would find him.
Article Summary: Solo sailor's Pacific Ocean voyage to Hawaii turned into a survival ordeal. Kai Sato left California's Catalina Islands on 7 June, beginning what he intended to be his first solo crossing of the Pacific to Hawaii. Only a couple of weeks into the voyage, everything changed. The sailboat's mast failed, removing the vessel's main source of power and leaving it at the mercy of wind and ocean currents.

Article Title: After a study explored covering 4,000 miles of California's canals with solar panels, a 1.6-megawatt pilot was completed in 2026
Article Text:
California is exploring solar panels over its extensive canal network. This initiative aims to reduce water evaporation and generate renewable electricity simultaneously. A pilot project called Project Nexus is currently evaluating this innovative approach. Image Credits: Turlock Irrigation District

Energy and water co-benefits from covering canals with solar panels

Why researchers looked above the canals instead of beside them

The study suggests significant water savings and electricity production potential. This technology offers a dual benefit by utilizing existing infrastructure. Image Credits: Energy and water co-benefits from covering canals with solar panels

From research to a working demonstration

California's extensive canal network delivers water to farms, communities and cities across the state, playing a central role in California's water distribution system for both agriculture and urban areas. However, because the waterways are open to the sun, considerable amounts of water can be lost through evaporation, particularly during periods of high temperatures and prolonged dry weather.A study published in Nature Sustainability , titled, explored whether a single approach could help address multiple challenges at once. The study examined the potential impact of installing solar panels above what the researchers described as California's approximately 6,350-kilometre (roughly 4,000-mile) canal network. Their analysis suggested that canal-top solar installations could generate renewable electricity while reducing water lost through evaporation and making better use of infrastructure that already exists.Rather than proposing that canal-top solar replace conventional solar farms, the study evaluated how it could complement other forms of renewable energy while avoiding the need for additional land in many locations.California has invested heavily in both water infrastructure and renewable energy over recent decades. At the same time, prolonged droughts and rising temperatures have increased concern about water security, while demand for clean electricity continues to grow.Instead of placing solar panels on agricultural land or undeveloped open spaces, the researchers evaluated the potential of installing them above existing canals.According to the Nature Sustainability study, the researchers found that shading from the panels could reduce evaporation and may also help limit the growth of aquatic weeds in some canals. The flowing water beneath the panels could also help cool the solar panels. Because solar panels generally become less efficient at higher temperatures, this cooling effect could improve electricity generation under certain conditions.According to the Nature Sustainability study, the researchers estimated that covering California's canal network with solar panels could save about 39,000 cubic metres of water per kilometre each year. Because the supporting structures would be built above existing canals, the approach could also reduce the need to convert additional land for renewable energy projects.The study suggests canal-top solar could offer benefits beyond electricity production. By making greater use of existing infrastructure corridors, the approach could help reduce competition for land in areas where agriculture, wildlife habitat and renewable energy development overlap.The researchers emphasised, however, that these findings were based on modelling and engineering analysis rather than large-scale deployment across California. Practical implementation would depend on construction costs, engineering design, site-specific conditions, maintenance requirements and other operational considerations.Project Nexus, a 1.6-megawatt solar-over-canal pilot in California's Central Valley, was completed and commissioned in 2025 to evaluate the performance of solar panels installed above active canals. California highlighted the project in an announcement published in April 2026According to the governor’s office, Project Nexus is backed by a $20 million investment and will be evaluated with partners from the California Department of Water Resources, Turlock Irrigation District, SolarAquaGrid LLC and UC Merced. The pilot is designed to measure electricity output, evaporation savings, possible water-quality gains and maintenance reductions, including lower vegetation growth along the canal.According to the California Governor's Office, Project Nexus will evaluate electricity generation, water savings from reduced evaporation, potential improvements in water quality and the feasibility of installing solar panels above active canals. Such projects allow engineers to compare real-world performance with earlier modelling and assess whether the technology could be expanded more widely.It evaluates the concept as one option that could contribute to broader efforts to improve water management while increasing renewable electricity generation.As a result, not every canal would necessarily be suitable for overhead solar installations. Decisions about future projects would need to consider engineering feasibility, maintenance access, local electricity demand and the characteristics of individual waterways.The Project Nexus pilot will help researchers and project partners assess how canal-top solar performs outside computer models, including its ability to generate electricity, reduce water losses and operate alongside existing irrigation infrastructure.
Article Summary: California's extensive canal network delivers water to farms, communities and cities across the state. Because the waterways are open to the sun, considerable amounts of water can be lost through evaporation, particularly during periods of high temperatures and prolonged dry weather. A study published in Nature Sustainability explored whether a single approach could help address multiple challenges at once.

Article Title: Pakistan minister invokes 'cockroaches' analogy, says united Gen-Z can 'turn everything upside down'
Article Text:
Calls for new provinces and decentralisation

'Biggest supporter' of democracy

Youth want jobs, not handouts

'Cockroaches' remark

Business community urged to back reforms

Mounting debt concerns

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think is more important for the youth? Merit-based jobs Welfare schemes Internships and training programs 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Pakistan interior minister Mohsin Naqvi on Thursday declared that the country's governance system had "collapsed", calling for the creation of new administrative units or provinces and urging political parties to reach a consensus on sweeping constitutional and governance reforms. He warned that without structural changes, Pakistan would remain trapped in recurring political and economic crises.Addressing the Pakistan Economic Summit 2026 in Islamabad, Naqvi said Pakistan's decades-old governance model had failed to deliver justice, economic opportunities or effective public services. He argued that decentralisation and the emergence of new leadership were essential to reform the country."Whether you agree or not, the system we have been living under has collapsed."Naqvi said repeated attempts to fix Pakistan's problems within the existing framework had failed, adding that the same debates would continue even a decade later unless the country's governance structure was fundamentally reformed."I believe the people responsible for bringing Pakistan to its current state are sitting in this hall," he said, adding that if a system had failed to function effectively for 70 to 80 years, there must be fundamental flaws in its design.The interior minister said the solution lay in decentralising governance through the creation of additional administrative units or provinces, arguing that local ownership would improve governance and allow new political leadership to emerge."The solution is only one.""You will have to take [the matter of] administrative units, provinces or whatever you may call it, to the public.""Unless units are made and they take ownership, and a new leadership comes, this will not happen."Naqvi urged all political parties to negotiate a comprehensive reform agenda instead of continuing with what he described as an outdated governance structure."All political parties should sit together in a single room, whether for a day, a month or a year. They will have to settle every issue of their country, including new units and provinces.""Unless they do so, unless they sit together and change this, this country will remain in the same condition, regardless of how many seminars and functions you hold."While describing himself as "the biggest supporter" of democracy, Naqvi argued that democratic governance could take different institutional forms and said Pakistan should not remain tied to a system that had consistently underperformed."We all want democracy. I am the biggest supporter of democracy and will remain so. But there are five or six systems within democracy. Yet we insist that no matter what happens, we must continue dragging along the same one."He also criticised policy failures, saying Pakistan continued to import agricultural commodities such as wheat despite being an agricultural country.Naqvi acknowledged the long working hours of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif but argued that the government remained focused on crisis management instead of long-term reforms."I have seen Shehbaz Sharif work 12 to 14 hours a day. He could even work 18 hours a day, but we are only firefighting.""Until you correct the basics of this country while adhering to the spirit of democracy, this will remain the same."Naqvi said Pakistan's young people were demanding merit-based employment, transparent recruitment and equal opportunities rather than welfare schemes or financial assistance."We think giving youngsters stipends of a few thousand rupees a month or tablets will make them happy, but ask them what they really want.""Their only demand is merit-based jobs and employment opportunities. They are not asking you for tablets or a few thousand rupees every month."According to the minister, Pakistani youth had the potential to earn between $2,000 and $4,000 per month if provided with the right opportunities.Referring to a term that has recently been used for Gen-Z in the wake of student protests in India, Naqvi warned that growing frustration among young people should not be ignored."If these 'Cockroaches' get united, they can turn everything upside down."He said the government should address the aspirations of young people before dissatisfaction intensified, arguing that their primary demands centred on merit-based jobs and equal opportunities.Naqvi also called on Pakistan's business community to play a more active role in reforming the country's political system, arguing that industrialists and traders had long been intertwined with politics."One gives funding of Rs500 million before elections, or the other gives Rs100 million or Rs50 million."He questioned why business leaders preferred financing political candidates instead of contesting elections themselves."Why don't businessmen enter politics? You are willing to fund politicians, but consider entering politics yourselves to be something shameful. You will have to stand up for yourselves."Highlighting Pakistan's fiscal challenges, Naqvi likened the federal government's finances to a household beginning every month already burdened with debt."The condition of this federal government is such that we make our budgets in the negative, and we discuss how much debt we have to incur this year.""[...] We will take more debts, but we will not correct things."He said leaders across the political spectrum understood the country's structural problems but had repeatedly failed to implement reforms, urging all stakeholders to build consensus on a long-term governance overhaul.
Article Summary: Mohsin Naqvi says Pakistan's governance system has "collapsed" Calls for creation of new administrative units or provinces. Urges political parties to reach consensus on constitutional and governance reforms. Calls on business community to play more active role in reforming the country.

Article Title: 34 killed as methane explosion tears through coal mine in Pakistan's Balochistan
Article Text:
Coal mine blast in Pakistan's Balochistan (AP photo)

At least 34 miners in Pakistan were killed and 10 other remained trapped after a methane gas explosion ripped through a coal mine in Balochistan province on Thursday, as officials told news agency AP.While rescuers continued a race against time to reach those still underground.The explosion took place on the outskirts of Quetta, the provincial capital, and was apparently triggered by a buildup of methane gas, according to government mine inspector Ghani Baloch.Rescue teams initially recovered the bodies of seven miners before locating 25 more, provincial officials and the disaster management agency said in a statement. The search and rescue operation was continuing as teams worked to locate and recover the remaining trapped workers.Baloch said rescue efforts would continue until all those trapped were accounted for, but warned that the death toll was likely to rise.“The chances of finding anyone alive diminish after methane gas explosions because oxygen levels drop to zero, and rescuers are also proceeding cautiously inside the mine,” Baloch said.Authorities have begun handing over the recovered bodies to their families for burial, while relatives of the missing miners continued to wait anxiously for updates, Baloch added.Balochistan's minister for mines and minerals Shoaib Nosherwani said rescue personnel were operating under extremely challenging conditions.Nosherwani expressed condolences to the victims' families and announced that the provincial government would provide compensation of 500,000 Pakistani rupees (about $1,800) to the family of each miner killed in the blast.He said authorities would conduct a thorough investigation into the cause of the explosion and review mining safety measures to prevent similar incidents.Meanwhile, the Pakistan Central Mines Labour Federation alleged that negligence may have contributed to the disaster. In a statement, the union urged the government to strictly enforce mining safety regulations and take stringent action against companies that violate mine safety laws.Fatal accidents are frequent in Pakistan's coal mining industry, particularly in Balochistan, where many mines operate without adequate ventilation, gas monitoring systems or other essential safety measures.Labour groups and mine workers have repeatedly accused mine owners of ignoring safety standards and failing to provide proper protective equipment.Despite the hazardous working conditions and meagre wages, thousands of people continue to rely on coal mining for their livelihoods in Balochistan, Pakistan's largest yet least developed province, where poverty and unemployment remain widespread.
Article Summary: The explosion took place on the outskirts of Quetta, the provincial capital, and was apparently triggered by a buildup of methane gas. Rescue teams initially recovered the bodies of seven miners before locating 25 more. The search and rescue operation was continuing as teams worked to locate and recover the remaining trapped workers.

Article Title: 11 police personnel, 15 militants killed in overnight attack in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
Article Text:
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (ANI file photo)

Pakistan suffered a major overnight militant attack on a police post in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, leaving 11 police personnel and 15 attackers dead by early Thursday.The attack targeted the Khazina police post in Hangu district, close to the Afghanistan border. Responding security forces fought back, killing 15 militants during the exchange of fire, police official Irfan Khan said.No group immediately claimed responsibility for the assault, though suspicion is expected to fall on the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which has intensified attacks on Pakistani security forces in the border region in recent months.The dead included police officer Diyar Khan, who was leading a reinforcement team to the attacked outpost, according to a statement from the provincial police. More than two dozen police personnel were also injured in the fighting.Police said the militants used heavy weapons to storm the post. Reinforcements heading to the scene were ambushed on the way, with an armoured personnel carrier damaged before officers regrouped and engaged the attackers, eventually forcing them back.Pakistan has seen a steady rise in militant violence in recent years, with the TTP blamed for many of the attacks. Although the group is separate from Afghanistan's ruling Taliban. Since the Taliban returned to power in Kabul in 2021, Islamabad has repeatedly accused the Afghan government of sheltering TTP militants, a charge that Kabul has consistently denied.
Article Summary: Attack targeted Khazina police post in Hangu district, close to the Afghanistan border. Responding security forces fought back, killing 15 militants during the exchange of fire. No group immediately claimed responsibility for the assault, though suspicion is expected to fall on the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP)

Article Title: 'Frustration of their failure': Ex-envoy Vidya Bhushan Soni slams Pakistan over PoK unrest
Article Text:
Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (ANI file photo)

NEW DELHI: As unrest intensified in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) during the region's ongoing elections, former Indian envoy to Ukraine Vidya Bhushan Soni said the protests reflected growing frustration among people over Pakistan's failure to address its economic and domestic challenges.His remarks came after Pakistan defence minister Khawaja Asif called people in PoK as "enemies like India".Speaking to news agency ANI, Soni said frustration was growing in Pakistan because the country had expected to benefit by projecting itself as a mediator in international affairs and hoped that would help it secure economic assistance. "I think again there is a frustration creeping in, in Pakistan. Because they thought that they were playing the mediator role and they thought things would be fine and they would be once again back into business in terms of getting some economic aid, etc. That's not happening," he said.Soni said several groups opposed to the Pakistani government, including Baloch groups and people in PoK, were now putting pressure on Islamabad because they believed the country had reached a difficult position. According to him, Pakistan was more focused on projecting itself internationally as a peaceful nation than solving the problems of its own people."They are the ones who feel that we must put the pressure because now Pakistan is pushed to the wall.And so that's why they are coming out on the street; they are showing their frustration, they're showing their anger, they're showing their patience is running thin," he said.He added that Pakistan should first address the concerns of its own citizens instead of trying to play a larger role on the global stage. "You have to do something about the people, their own people, rather than trying to go and solve the world's problem; first you solve your own problem back home," Soni said.Warning that the unrest was unlikely to end anytime soon, Soni alleged that Pakistan could respond by using force against its own people because its priorities remained focused on international issues. "It has consequences; it will not stop because Pakistan's priority still continues to be international, and they will try to come down heavily through the use of force on their own people," he said.Calling the situation in PoK particularly worrying, Soni said many residents felt their grievances were being ignored, which had deepened their frustration. "The worrisome factor right now is POK because they have seen that their case is not being heard; they are totally ignored. So I feel that it's a frustration of their failure," he said.Meanwhile, the Jammu Kashmir Joint Awami Action Committee (JKAAC), through a series of posts on X, raised concerns over the treatment of injured people and the presence of masked individuals in civilian clothing alongside police personnel during the crackdown. "The treatment of the injured and the presence of masked individuals in civilian clothing alongside police officers raise serious concerns that require urgent scrutiny," the group said.The committee also alleged that civilian property had been damaged during the operation, saying, "The destruction of civilian property raises serious concerns about the conduct of the security forces during the ongoing crackdown." It further claimed that surveillance equipment had been deliberately destroyed, adding, "The deliberate destruction of surveillance equipment raises serious concerns about transparency, accountability, and the preservation of evidence. "Calling for international attention, the JKAAC urged the United Nations, international media, diplomatic missions and human rights organisations to examine the footage from the clashes and launch an independent probe. "We call on the United Nations, international media, diplomatic missions, and international human rights organisations to examine this footage, independently verify the facts, and support an immediate, independent and impartial international investigation into the recent events in Pakistan-occupied Jammu & Kashmir," the group said.
Article Summary: Former Indian envoy to Ukraine Vidya Bhushan Soni says protests reflect Pakistan's failure to address its economic and domestic challenges. Soni said frustration was growing in Pakistan because the country had expected to benefit by projecting itself as a mediator in international affairs. Pakistan defence minister Khawaja Asif called people in PoK as "enemies like India"

Article Title: Is Pakistan facilitating Chinese missile shipments to Iran? Islamabad responds
Article Text:
Pakistan army chief Asim Munir (AP file photo)

Pakistan has pushed back strongly against reports claiming it would act as a conduit for Chinese-made weapons headed to Iran, as Tehran remains locked in a tense standoff with the Donald Trump-led US administration.The rejection by Munir's military comes as Islamabad continues its familiar balancing act, staying aligned with China while courting Trump-led Washington, exposing its two-faced tendency in its foreign policy approach.Pakistan’s military chief has recently found favour with US President Donald Trump , while Islamabad continues to project itself as a potential bridge between its neighbour Iran and the United States.Reacting to reports that Pakistan was set to facilitate the transit of up to 400 Chinese-made shoulder-fired air defence missile systems to Iran, the Trump's "favourite field marshal"-led army dismissed the claims outright.“All such speculations are baseless and devoid of truth,” Pakistan’s military media wing, the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), said, according to Azerbaijan news, citing Anadolu Agency.“Such speculations are categorically rejected,” the ISPR added.The denial came after Reuters reported on Wednesday that Iran was expected to receive its first shipment of Chinese air defence systems within weeks, as Tehran looks to rebuild its defensive capabilities amid its conflict with the United States.According to Reuters, the initial deliveries were planned to move from Urumqi in western China and pass through Pakistan before reaching Iran, citing unnamed sources familiar with the matter. The sources, however, did not clarify whether the transit would take place by air or through land routes.The reports emerged amid speculation over US weapons stockpiles being stretched due to ongoing global conflicts, though Trump later dismissed such concerns. The episode has once again highlighted Islamabad’s delicate balancing act between Beijing and Washington as tensions continue to rise around Iran.
Article Summary: Pakistan denies reports it would act as a conduit for Chinese-made weapons headed to Iran. Comes as Islamabad continues its familiar balancing act, staying aligned with China while courting Trump-led Washington. Islamabad continues to project itself as a potential bridge between its neighbour Iran and the United States.

Article Title: Security forces’ crackdown, civil unrest continue in POK, 20 dead
Article Text:
File photo: PoK unrest

The situation in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir ( POK ) remains volatile amid mass civilian unrest, election-related violence, and heavy crackdowns by Pakistani security forces. According to sources, Pakistani forces used lethal force against Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) during their long march from Rawalakot to Muzaffarabad.The crackdown reportedly resulted in the deaths of 20 civilians and left over 33 protesters injured.Amnesty International USA said that the disturbing reports emerging from Rawalakot were consistent with Pakistani authorities’ “long history of unlawful violence against protesters”. “We urge the Pakistani authorities torestore all communications access and allow media and independent observers into the area,” it said.While security forces continue to maintain a heightened presence in Rawalakot, Muzaffarabad and other areas, sources said the possibility of additional protests remains high over the coming days because of declining public confidence in the political process.Local authorities have also continued to impose communication blackouts and suspended services across POK.
Article Summary: Pakistani forces used lethal force against Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) during their long march from Rawalakot to Muzaffarabad. The crackdown reportedly resulted in the deaths of 20 civilians and left over 33 protesters injured. Article Title: Ex-PM Imran Khan's sister charged under cybercrime law over remarks on Pakistan army, India conflict
Article Text: NEW DELHI: Pakistan's anti-cybercrime agency has registered an FIR against Noreen Niazi, sister of jailed former prime minister Imran Khan , over remarks about the Pakistan military and last year's four-day conflict with India, an official said on Wednesday.The case was registered by the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) in Islamabad under Sections 20 and 26-A of the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA), nearly 10 days after the agency summoned Niazi for questioning over social media content it described as "false, offensive and inflammatory"."NCCIA in Islamabad has registered a case against Noreen Niazi, the sister of former prime minister Imran Khan, under the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA)," an official told PTI.According to the FIR, Niazi made false and baseless allegations against Pakistan and its armed forces."Noreen Niazi attempted to undermine public confidence in the state and create panic among the people. She disseminated false, provocative, insulting and threatening content and conducted a systematic propaganda campaign against state and security institutions," the FIR said.The case stems from an interview that was widely circulated on social media, in which Niazi claimed the May 2025 India-Pakistan military confrontation was the result of collusion between Pakistan's military leadership and Prime Minister Narendra Modi and was orchestrated to enhance the image of Pakistan's armed forces.She also questioned Pakistan's military response during the four-day conflict that followed the Pahalgam terror attack and claimed, without providing evidence, that India deliberately refrained from escalating the conflict because Pakistan was moving towards recognising Israel and that the episode was intended to facilitate Islamabad's entry into the Abraham Accords."What do you think? ... India, which is a big country, was not in position to respond to Pakistan when it attacked on May 10?" Niazi said in the interview. "It could have but India deliberately refrained from giving a strong response because of some understanding."Pakistan's NCCIA had issued summons to Niazi on July 18, directing her to appear before investigators to record her statement in connection with the inquiry.
Article Summary: Pakistan's anti-cybercrime agency has registered an FIR against Noreen Niazi, sister of jailed former prime minister Imran Khan. The case stems from an interview that was widely circulated on social media, in which she claimed the May 2025 India-Pakistan military confrontation was the result of collusion between Pakistan's military leadership.

Article Title: 'They're enemies like India': Pakistan minister Khawaja Asif justifies killing of over 30 protesters in PoK
Article Text:
"I put the protesters of PojK in the same category as India and consider them as enemies," Khawaja Asif said.

Pakistan defence minister Khawaja Asif said he considered protesters in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoJK) enemies, just as he considered India."I put the protesters of PojK in the same category as India and consider them as enemies," Khawaja Asif said when asked about the protest that intensified on Monday leading to the killing of over 30 protesters.Moreover, the Amnesty International USA called the Pakistani crackdown on protestors as "disturbing" and urged Islamabad to "restore all communications access and allow media and independent observers into the area.""The disturbing reports emerging from Rawalakot are consistent with the Pakistani authorities’ long history of unlawful violence against protesters in PoJK. We urge the Pakistani authorities to restore all communications access and allow media and independent observers into the area," Amnesty International USA posted on X.The protest erupted as thousands of demonstrators began marching towards Muzaffarabad after negotiations between the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) and the authorities broke down, while election officials postponed legislative assembly polls in two districts amid the unrest.The political crisis unfolded alongside the first phase of polling in 13 constituencies of the Mirpur division. However, political parties said the prolonged demonstrations had severely affected electioneering across the region.Campaign rallies, public meetings and door-to-door outreach have reportedly been disrupted by strikes and sit-ins, while candidates have expressed uncertainty over voter participation if the protests continue.Residents told local media that public interest in the elections had sharply declined, with many believing that longstanding grievances and basic rights should be addressed before any electoral exercise. According to several residents, enthusiasm for the polls is "almost non-existent," with the protest movement taking precedence over electoral politics.The ongoing agitation follows weeks of growing tensions in the region. On June 30, the JAAC criticised Pakistani authorities after an opposition delegation was reportedly prevented from entering PoJK, calling it another example of restrictions on democratic rights and political dissent.The committee also alleged that authorities had obstructed food supplies and curtailed access to the region, claims it said reflected the government's approach towards the people of PoJK.
Article Summary: Pakistan defence minister Khawaja Asif said he considered protesters in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoJK) enemies, just as he considered India. Amnesty International USA called the Pakistani crackdown on protestors as "disturbing" and urged Islamabad to "restore all communications access"

Article Title: PoK protests: Thousands march to Muzaffarabad after failed talks; polls delayed in two districts
Article Text:
Thousands march to Muzaffarabad after failed talks; polls delayed in two districts

Talks collapse, protesters hit the streets

Elections overshadowed by unrest

Protests in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) intensified on Monday as thousands of demonstrators began marching towards Muzaffarabad after negotiations between the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) and the authorities broke down, while election officials postponed legislative assembly polls in two districts amid the unrest.The Election Commission deferred voting in the Sudhnoti and Rawalakot constituencies until August 10, citing an ongoing sit-in led by the Public Action Committee (PAC).The postponement comes as a weeks-long protest movement continues to disrupt public life and cast uncertainty over the electoral process.The latest escalation followed the collapse of talks between JAAC leaders and the government on Saturday. Protest organisers alleged that authorities refused to release detained activists, withdraw criminal cases against protesters or agree to the committee's core demands.After the negotiations failed, JAAC issued an ultimatum, asking the government to formally notify acceptance of its demands by 1pm on July 27. It warned that if no action was taken, thousands of supporters would march from Rawalakot to Muzaffarabad — a call that was subsequently carried out.The demonstrations mark the latest phase of a protest campaign that has entered its 52nd day.The political crisis unfolded alongside the first phase of polling in 13 constituencies of the Mirpur division. However, political parties said the prolonged demonstrations had severely affected electioneering across the region.Campaign rallies, public meetings and door-to-door outreach have reportedly been disrupted by strikes and sit-ins, while candidates have expressed uncertainty over voter participation if the protests continue.Residents told local media that public interest in the elections had sharply declined, with many believing that longstanding grievances and basic rights should be addressed before any electoral exercise. According to several residents, enthusiasm for the polls is "almost non-existent," with the protest movement taking precedence over electoral politics.The ongoing agitation follows weeks of growing tensions in the region. On June 30, the JAAC criticised Pakistani authorities after an opposition delegation was reportedly prevented from entering PoK, calling it another example of restrictions on democratic rights and political dissent.The committee also alleged that authorities had obstructed food supplies and curtailed access to the region, claims it said reflected the government's approach towards the people of PoK.Meanwhile, Amnesty International has criticised Pakistan's handling of the situation ahead of the regional elections, accusing the authorities of using heavy-handed measures to suppress peaceful political dissent and violate fundamental human rights.
Article Summary: Thousands march to Muzaffarabad after failed talks; polls delayed in two districts. Election Commission deferred voting in the Sudhnoti and Rawalakot constituencies until August 10, citing an ongoing sit-in led by the Public Action Committee (PAC)

Article Title: Saudi money, Chinese weapons, American patronage: Can Pakistan balance all three?
Article Text:
Saudi Arabia Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman Al Saud (MBS), Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir Ahmed Shah, US President Donald Trump, President Xi Jinping.

Pakistan's foreign policy paradox: Punching above its weight while struggling at home

China, Saudi Arabia and US: The three pillars of Pakistan's diplomacy





Rebuilding ties with Washington under Trump





Pakistan's role as mediator between Washington and Tehran





Growing security cooperation with Saudi Arabia

Domestic troubles threaten Pakistan's global ambitions





Munir's 'hard state' vision

NEW DELHI: Pakistan is attempting one of its most ambitious foreign policy balancing acts in decades, seeking to simultaneously preserve its strategic partnership with China, deepen security ties with Saudi Arabia, rebuild relations with US President Donald Trump 's administration, mediate between Washington and Tehran, and strengthen coordination with Turkey and Egypt, according to a detailed Financial Times report.The report says Pakistan's military leadership under Field Marshal Asim Munir believes the country's geopolitical location and longstanding relationships across competing power centres have created a rare opportunity to elevate Islamabad's diplomatic profile despite mounting economic and security challenges at home.According to the report, Pakistan's efforts have become particularly visible during the recent Middle East crisis, with Islamabad attempting to position itself as a regional mediator while simultaneously expanding defence cooperation with Gulf monarchies and maintaining its decades-old strategic partnership with Beijing.However, analysts quoted by the newspaper warn that Pakistan's expanding diplomatic ambitions are unfolding against the backdrop of a fragile economy, worsening militancy and growing political repression, raising questions about whether Islamabad can sustain such an ambitious foreign policy.According to the report, Pakistan today finds itself pursuing an unusually complex foreign policy that requires it to balance sometimes competing strategic relationships.The newspaper says Islamabad is simultaneously:Former Pakistani brigadier Feroz Khan, quoted by the FT, says Pakistan has increasingly relied on diplomacy and military influence to compensate for its domestic weaknesses."Given its deep economic and political weaknesses, [Pakistan's] nuclear bomb, its conventional military forces and diplomacy are all it has to punch above its weight as a middle power," says Khan, who now teaches at the Naval Postgraduate School in California.According to the newspaper, Pakistan's military establishment believes the Middle East offers Islamabad greater strategic space than South Asia, where India's economic and military strength limits Pakistan's regional influence."As a south Asian power, Pakistan is permanently number two to India, the wealthier, stronger and more useful nation to the US in that region," Khan says. "But in the Middle East, it believes it can come into its own, with the blessing of US Central Command and Saudi Arabia."The report says Islamabad's diplomatic outreach has coincided with efforts by Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Turkey to play larger roles in shaping the region's post-war security architecture.According to analysts cited by the newspaper, this emerging grouping could eventually serve as a counterweight to growing military cooperation involving the United Arab Emirates, Israel and India.According to FT, one of the clearest illustrations of Pakistan's growing role came shortly before Islamabad hosted talks involving the United States and Iran earlier this year.The newspaper reports that on April 10, Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed al-Jadaan visited Islamabad and met Pakistan's military chief Field Marshal Asim Munir at the Prime Minister House.Citing two people briefed on the discussions, FT says Saudi Arabia requested Pakistan's military support as the kingdom came under missile and drone attacks allegedly launched by Iran.According to the report, Riyadh had already signed a mutual defence agreement with Islamabad in 2025 and wanted Pakistan to provide personnel and military equipment.The newspaper says Pakistan's leadership was initially reluctant because such a move could complicate its planned mediation efforts between Washington and Tehran and trigger domestic political criticism from sections of Pakistan's population sympathetic to Iran.However, according to the report, Pakistan was also under severe financial pressure.The report says that
