diplomat said.According to the newspaper, Munir has increasingly concentrated power within Pakistan's military establishment since becoming army chief in November 2022.The Pakistan's parliament has granted him expanded authority, including extending his tenure and giving him greater oversight over the armed forces while critics accuse the government of weakening judicial independence and restricting political dissent.Analysts quoted by the newspaper argue that Munir believes tighter military control is necessary to restore order after years of political instability and economic decline.Yet, according to the report, Pakistan's growing diplomatic activism abroad contrasts sharply with the challenges confronting the country at home, including rising militant violence, slowing investment, mounting debt and increasing dependence on external financial assistance.According to the FT, Pakistan's current foreign policy rests on maintaining close ties with three major powers whose interests often diverge: China, Saudi Arabia and the United States.The newspaper says Beijing remains Islamabad's largest defence supplier and one of its most important strategic partners, while Saudi Arabia has become Pakistan's principal financial backer. At the same time, Pakistan has worked to rebuild ties with Washington under US President Donald Trump, despite decades of fluctuating relations.Pakistan military spokesperson Lt Gen Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry told the Financial Times that Islamabad's relationships with Beijing and Riyadh differ from conventional diplomatic partnerships."There are two countries with whom Pakistan has a special relationship: China and Saudi Arabia," Chaudhry said. "With them, there is never a quid pro quo."According to FT report, China has invested more than $30 billion in Pakistan through infrastructure, transport and power projects, including development of the strategically important Gwadar Port under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC). Beijing has also played a central role in Pakistan's nuclear, missile and defence programmes over several decades and continues to be its largest supplier of military equipment.Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, remains Pakistan's biggest financial lifeline, according to the report. Besides repeated loans and deferred payment facilities, Riyadh has frequently rolled over debt repayments to help Islamabad avoid a balance-of-payments crisis.The Pakistan currently owes Saudi Arabia around $8 billion, equivalent to nearly 46 per cent of the country's central bank reserves, making the Gulf kingdom one of Islamabad's most important creditors.The FT report says Pakistan has also sought to restore relations with the United States after years of strained ties.According to the newspaper, Islamabad nominated Donald Trump for the Nobel Peace Prize in June last year for what it described as his "decisive diplomatic intervention" during Pakistan's brief military conflict with India.The report notes that Trump, who had once accused Pakistan of giving the United States "nothing but lies and deceit", has since publicly referred to Asim Munir as his "favourite field marshal", reflecting what the newspaper describes as one of the warmest periods in US-Pakistan relations in recent years.Accroding to the report, Washington also gave Pakistan greater diplomatic space during the recent Middle East crisis.Asfandyar Mir, senior fellow for South Asia at the Stimson Center in Washington, told the newspaper Munir had taken a considerable political gamble by placing Pakistan at the centre of diplomatic efforts."Munir took a significant risk by staking his standing on diplomacy that could easily have backfired," Mir said."But Trump, in a departure from the India-centric consensus that has defined American policy for a decade, allowed Pakistan to make its play."According to the report, Pakistan viewed improved ties with Washington as essential not only for regional diplomacy but also for maintaining access to Western financial institutions at a time when the country's economy remains heavily dependent on IMF support.According to the Financial Times, Pakistan attempted to use its relationships with both Iran and the United States to position itself as a neutral intermediary during the recent conflict.The newspaper reports that Asim Munir chaired marathon discussions between US Vice President JD Vance and Iranian representatives that eventually laid the groundwork for what the report describes as the "Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding", a 14-point ceasefire agreement.However, according to the Financial Times, those diplomatic gains proved short-lived after President Trump later declared the ceasefire "over" following renewed Iranian attacks on commercial shipping and authorised fresh military strikes.The newspaper says Tehran responded with missile and drone attacks against Gulf states while once again disrupting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route through which most of Pakistan's imported oil passes.Despite the renewed conflict, Pakistan's military insists Islamabad continues to pursue diplomacy."Pakistan has a clear interest in peace in the larger Muslim world, and particularly the Gulf," Chaudhry told the Financial Times. "The countries of the Gulf know this and are therefore more comfortable dealing with us as a security partner and honest broker."The military spokesperson also said Pakistan had remained engaged with all major regional stakeholders."Pakistan has been working with all of the stakeholders in the Gulf as well as Iran to ensure that this war should not spiral and should not expand," Chaudhry said.The Financial Times says Pakistan's mediation efforts have coincided with rapidly expanding military cooperation with Saudi Arabia.According to the report, the two countries signed a mutual defence agreement in September 2025 that has not been made public but was approved without parliamentary debate.The newspaper says official statements from both governments described the agreement as stating that "any aggression against either country shall be considered an aggression against both."According to a person briefed on the discussions, cited by the Financial Times, Islamabad and Riyadh are also exploring the creation of a joint aerial defence system following vulnerabilities exposed during attacks on Saudi infrastructure.The newspaper says closer defence cooperation also serves Pakistan's own economic interests.More than 5.5 million Pakistanis work across Gulf countries, sending home over $20 billion annually in remittances that remain one of Pakistan's largest sources of foreign exchange.Umer Karim of the Riyadh-based King Faisal Centre for Research and Islamic Studies told the Financial Times that Saudi Arabia has repeatedly acted as Pakistan's financial backstop."In Saudi Arabia, you have a state which will always at least try to provide you with a degree of financial cushion in moments of great need," Karim said.The Financial Times says Pakistan's increasingly close relationship with Saudi Arabia also exposes Islamabad to new strategic vulnerabilities.According to the report, Pakistan remains heavily dependent on Saudi financial assistance while also sharing deep religious, cultural and historical ties with neighbouring Iran.The newspaper notes that Pakistan is home to one of the world's largest Shia populations, estimated at around 40 million, making any perceived tilt towards Riyadh politically sensitive.According to the Financial Times, tensions became particularly evident after the assassination of Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei earlier this year, which reportedly triggered riots in several Pakistani cities that left at least two dozen people dead.The report also says Pakistan faced additional financial pressure when the United Arab Emirates demanded immediate repayment of $3.5 billion in loans, reflecting what analysts describe as growing geopolitical competition within the Gulf.Karim warned that Pakistan's dependence on Saudi Arabia could eventually leave it with limited diplomatic flexibility."Considering Pakistan's indispensable financial dependence on Saudi Arabia, it essentially won't have much of a choice," he told the Financial Times.The newspaper concludes that Pakistan's attempt to simultaneously retain Chinese strategic support, Saudi financial backing and improved relations with Washington represents one of the most complex balancing acts in its modern diplomatic history.However, analysts quoted throughout the report caution that sustaining such a strategy will ultimately depend on Islamabad's ability to stabilise its economy, improve internal security and reduce its dependence on foreign creditors.While Pakistan has attempted to expand its diplomatic influence abroad, the Financial Times says the country's domestic challenges remain severe and could ultimately limit Islamabad's ability to sustain its ambitious foreign policy.According to the newspaper, Pakistan's economy continues to struggle under mounting debt, repeated balance-of-payments crises and dependence on international lenders. The country of around 255 million people has received 25 IMF bailout programmes, while official poverty climbed to a decade high of 29 per cent last year.The Financial Times says Pakistan also continues to battle a deteriorating security environment. Security forces are fighting Baloch separatist groups and the Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), both of which have intensified attacks in the country's western regions, disrupting plans to develop mineral-rich provinces and attract foreign investment.Critics quoted by the newspaper argue that Islamabad's growing diplomatic profile cannot compensate for deep-rooted domestic weaknesses."What good is a bigger voice on the world stage if the house is on fire?" former Pakistani ambassador to the United States and the United Kingdom Maleeha Lodhi told the Financial Times."Pakistan needs to fix the cracks within."According to the Financial Times, Field Marshal Asim Munir has sought to address Pakistan's internal instability by transforming the country into what he describes as a "hard state."The newspaper says Munir believes stronger military control is necessary to restore law and order, eliminate militancy, end years of political instability and create conditions for economic recovery.One former US diplomat who dealt extensively with Munir described the army chief's governing style in stark terms."Munir aspires to turn Pakistan into what he calls a 'hard state' and rules Pakistan with a 'massive chip on his shoulder'," the former diplomat told the Financial Times.According to the report, Munir, who became Pakistan's army chief in November 2022, has steadily expanded the military's influence over civilian institutions.The Financial Times says Pakistan's parliament has extended his tenure, granted him greater authority over the armed forces and backed legislation that critics say has weakened judicial independence and curtailed public criticism of the military.The newspaper notes that Munir and his supporters blame years of civilian-led governments for Pakistan's political instability and economic decline.The Financial Times says Pakistan's diplomatic ambitions ultimately depend on economic strength that the country has yet to achieve.According to the World Bank data cited by the newspaper, Pakistan spends substantially less than comparable lower-middle-income countries on health and education, leaving around 25 million children out of school. Nearly 78 per cent of children are unable to read at the expected level by the age of 10, while around 40 per cent suffer from stunted growth.Although the IMF recently praised Pakistan's implementation of its $7 billion bailout programme, the Financial Times says the country's debt burden remains overwhelming.According to Fitch Ratings, interest payments alone are expected to consume around 40 per cent of government revenues by the financial year ending June 2027.The newspaper reports that Pakistan has also sought $10 billion in financial assistance from Washington to strengthen its foreign exchange reserves.Despite official projections of 3.7 per cent economic growth, Pakistan's trade deficit has widened to a four-year high of $39.6 billion, driven by weak exports, rising imports and higher global commodity prices linked to the conflict in the Gulf.Stefan Dercon, an Oxford professor advising Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on economic reforms, warned that policymakers recognise the urgency of the situation."There's a small group of decision makers... that realise if they don't fix this economy, they will fall off the cliff of a deep economic and even political crisis," he told the Financial Times.
Article Summary: Pakistan's foreign policy paradox: Punching above its weight while struggling at home. Mediating between Iran and the United States. Deepening defence ties with Saudi Arabia. Maintaining its strategic partnership with China.Rebuilding relations with Donald Trump's administration. Coordinating closely with Turkey and Egypt on regional security issues.

Article Title: Pakistan: At least 15 killed in suicide attack on Khyber Pakhtunkhwa security check post
Article Text: At least 15 people, including 14 security personnel, were killed after terrorists attacked a joint police check post in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on Friday, the military said.According to Pakistan's Inter-Services Public Relations, the attack took place in the Tank district and was carried out by the Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP).ISPR said the attackers initially attempted to breach the check post's perimeter but were repelled by security forces."The attackers attempted to breach the check post's perimeter, but their attempts were swiftly and decisively foiled by the vigilant and resolute response of security forces," the military's media wing said.The security personnel engaged the militants and killed 15 terrorists during the exchange of fire, it added.The attackers then rammed an explosives-laden vehicle into the perimeter wall of the check post, triggering a powerful blast that caused extensive damage to the facility."Due to blast impact, infrastructure at the check post was seriously damaged; resultantly, 15 brave sons of the soil, including 12 military personnel, two policemen and a government official from the forest department, rendered the ultimate sacrifice and embraced shahadat (martyrdom)," the statement said.The ISPR said a sanitisation operation was underway to track down any remaining militants in the area. It added that Pakistan's security forces would continue counter-terrorism operations under the "Azm-i-Istehkam" campaign."These sacrifices of our brave soldiers further reinforce our unwavering commitment to safeguarding our nation at all costs," the statement added.The attack comes amid a spike in militant violence in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.Last week, the ISPR said security forces killed 24 militants in Bannu district and adjoining areas during intelligence-based operations following a recent surge in attacks targeting police and civilians.Earlier in May, at least 15 police personnel were killed in a suicide attack on the Fateh Khel police post in Bannu after militants rammed an explosives-laden vehicle into the facility.
Article Summary: At least 15 people, including 14 security personnel, were killed in the attack. The attack took place in the Tank district and was carried out by the Tehreek-i- Taliban Pakistan. The attackers initially attempted to breach the check post's perimeter but were repelled by security forces.

Article Title: Nepal communal violence: Three killed, curfew widens; PM Balendra Shah appeals for calm
Article Text:
Poll Vote & Share your view What is the best way to maintain peace during communal tensions? Dialogue and understanding Stronger security measures 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Nepal prime minister Balendra Shah on Thursday appealed for unity, restraint and social harmony after at least three people were killed in communal violence that began in Sunsari district and later spread to neighbouring Madhesh province. The violence prompted authorities to expand curfews and tighten security across several districts.Addressing the nation for the first time since the violence erupted, Shah said the government was treating the situation with its "full seriousness and sensitivity" and pledged a fair and transparent investigation into the clashes."The Government of Nepal is completely serious and sensitive about the tragic incident that took place in Dewanganj, Siraha and other places in Sunsari a few days ago and the turbulent atmosphere that has arisen in some districts since then," Shah said in the televised address.The government's response comes amid curfews, prohibitory orders and heightened security deployments in Sunsari, Siraha, Dhanusa and Parsa districts. Since Sunday, protests and tensions have spread across Nepal's southern plains, raising concerns over wider communal friction in areas bordering India.Violence spread to neighbouring Madhesh province on Thursday, where a teenager died during clashes in Golbazar market in Siraha district.Officials also confirmed that a person injured in the earlier violence in Sunsari succumbed to injuries in Koshi province, taking the death toll to three.According to officials, the unrest began late on Sunday in Ward No. 3 of Dewanganj rural municipality in Sunsari district after a dispute between local groups over loud music during preparations for the Bol Bam pilgrimage to the Saptakoshi River. AFPreported that tensions escalated over loud music and religious flags during a Hindu procession, prompting police to open fire to disperse the crowd, according to local official Poshan Lamichhane.The confrontation escalated into stone-pelting and violence, prompting police to intervene with batons, tear gas, warning shots and eventually live fire by the Armed Police Force. One person died on the spot from gunshot injuries, while several others were critically injured.Shah announced that the ministry of home affairs had formed an investigation committee and assured the public that those responsible would be prosecuted."As soon as the incident happened, all security agencies immediately reached the spot and made continuous efforts to normalise the situation, prevent further unpleasant incidents and maintain peace and security. The Ministry of Home Affairs has formed an investigation committee to conduct a fair investigation into the incident and take strict legal action against the culprits." he said.The prime minister said the government had adopted a multi-pronged approach to restore normalcy. He said an all-party meeting had been convened at the central level, while continuous dialogue was under way with local representatives, civil society members, religious leaders, community representatives and social activists."In addition, a meeting of the National Security Council has been convened to seriously review the overall peace and security situation in the country and necessary decisions have been taken according to the situation," Shah said.In his four-and-a-half-minute televised address, Shah also urged citizens not to circulate misinformation or inflammatory content that could worsen tensions." The essence of all religions is compassion, mercy, love and peace. Blaming an entire community for an unexpected and tragic incident in one part of the country and spreading the fire of revenge for it in other parts of the country cannot be justified or justified from any perspective," he said.Concluding his address in both Nepali and Maithili, Shah appealed for collective efforts to restore peace and preserve national unity."Our history is a witness that even in the most difficult and difficult situations, mutual unity, tolerance and conscience have become our greatest strength. We all have to play the role of responsible citizens and remove the clouds of unrest that have hung over this beautiful and peaceful Nepali sky. We, the common citizens, civil society, religious communities, all respected leaders, all political parties and responsible media, are making a heartfelt appeal to the government to exercise patience and restraint and maintain peace, harmony, brotherhood and national unity," he said.
Article Summary: Nepal's prime minister Balendra Shah appeals for unity, restraint and social harmony. Shah says the government is treating the situation with its "full seriousness and sensitivity" The violence prompted authorities to expand curfews and tighten security across several districts.

Article Title: 10 climbers, including Nirmal Purja, missing after avalanche on Broad Peak in PoK's Gilgit-Baltistan
Article Text:
Who is Nirmal Purja?

Four bodies have been recovered by Pakistani authorities out of the ten international climbers who had gone missing after an avalanche struck Broad Peak, one of the world's highest mountains in Pakistan-occupied Gilgit-Baltistan. The list of climbers includes world renowned Nepal-born mountaineer Nirmal Purja According to the Alpine Club of Pakistan, the avalanche hit the expedition around midday on Thursday on the 8,047-metre (26,400-foot) Broad Peak in the Karakoram range, the Associated Press reported.The team comprised of five Nepalese climbers, Pakistani mountaineer Sohail Sakhi from Hunza, Omani climber Nathira, American climber Mallory Geis, a Chinese climber identified only as Wang, and another foreign climber, the club said.The team has remained out of communication since the incident. However, a tracking device carried by Purja has continued to show movement, offering a glimmer of hope as rescuers race against time to reach the team.Speaking to Kantipur on Friday, Purja's business partner and Nepal lawmaker Mingma Gyabu Sherpa said data from the mountaineer's tracking device indicated that his location had changed after the avalanche."Initially, it appeared that he had been swept downhill by the avalanche," Sherpa was quoted as saying by The Kathmandu Post. "But after the point where the tracking had stopped, the location appears to have shifted again."Sherpa cautioned that the tracking data could not confirm Purja's condition but said it suggested some movement after the avalanche. He added that detailed information about the incident reached them only on Thursday evening, several hours after the avalanche struck.Poor weather has so far prevented helicopters from taking off, delaying aerial search-and-rescue operations. Sherpa said authorities were preparing to deploy helicopters on Friday morning if weather conditions improved.The club said it was working closely with government authorities to launch an immediate search-and-rescue operation. Its president, Maj Gen Irfan Arshad, and senior officials are coordinating efforts to mobilise helicopters and other rescue resources as soon as weather and operational conditions permit.Purja, also known as Nims Dai, is a Nepal-born British mountaineer and former Royal Marine. He joined the British Army in 2003 and became a Royal Marine in 2009.He rose to global prominence in 2019 after climbing all 14 of the world's 8,000-metre peaks in just 189 days, setting a record at the time.His achievement was later featured in the Netflix documentary "14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible." The record was surpassed in 2023 by a Norwegian climber and her Nepali Sherpa guide.Purja began his mountaineering career in 2012 after trekking to the Everest Base Camp. Instead of returning home as planned, he decided to climb Mount Everest , marking the start of his career as a high-altitude climber.
Article Summary: Four bodies have been recovered by Pakistani authorities out of the ten international climbers who had gone missing after an avalanche struck Broad Peak. The list of climbers includes world renowned Nepal-born mountaineer Nirmal Purja. A tracking device carried by Purja has continued to show movement, offering a glimmer of hope as rescuers race against time.

Article Title: Parliamentary committee seeks normalisation of visa operations in Bangladesh, govt says Hasina not allowed to undertake any political activity
Article Text:
Parl committee seeks normalisation of visa operations in Bangladesh, govt says Hasina not allowed to undertake any political activity

A Parliamentary committee on external affairs expressed concern that reduced visa processing volumes for Bangladesh nationals and security-related disruptions may adversely affect public perception and impede people-to-people engagement, which is vital for fostering bilateral ties.The Committee also noted the government's position that while providing refuge to former PM Sheikh Hasina , it had strictly adhered to the principle that no political activity is directed against any other country from Indian territory. The committee was informed by the government that it does not provide her with a political platform or any space to undertake any political activity from Indian territory.Recognizing the importance of sustained inter-personal contact for preserving mutual trust and confidence, the committee urged that the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) to work with security agencies and progressively normalize visa operations in Bangladesh "as soon as the situation permits"It also urged the ministry to develop a bilateral consular cooperation mechanism to periodically review visa policy, address grievances, and ensure that legitimate travellers are not subjected to various inconveniences, while maintaining necessary security safeguards. These recommendations were included in the Action Taken by the Government on the Observations/ Recommendations contained in the Ninth Report of the Committee on the subject ‘Future of India-Bangladesh Relationship’.Following the events of 5 August, 2024, that led to Hasina's exit, visa services were significantly scaled down, and consular personnel were withdrawn from Bangladesh. The MEA told the committee that1,500 visas are currently being issued each day across five centers in Bangladesh with medical visas accounting for approximately 80% of the total visas issued."The evolving security situation is under continuous review, and any decision on increasing daily issuance of visas or operationalizing additional visa centers will be taken in coordination with the relevant ministries of the government of India," it said.On the Hasina issue, the committee noted that the stay of Hasina in the country and India’s approach in this regard is guided by its civilizational ethos and humanitarian tradition of offering refuge to individuals facing circumstances of grave distress or existential threat.Taking note also of Dhaka's request for her extradition, the committee recommended that the government continue to uphold its principled and humanitarian approach, consistent with India’s "values and international responsibilities, while ensuring that such situations are managed with due sensitivity".
Article Summary: A Parliamentary committee on external affairs expressed concern that reduced visa processing volumes for Bangladesh nationals may adversely affect public perception. The Committee also noted the government's position that while providing refuge to former PM Sheikh Hasina, it had strictly adhered to the principle that no political activity is directed against any other country.

Article Title: Need to address some irritations in Bangladesh-India relations: Dhaka
Article Text:
File photo: Bangladeshi foreign minister Khalilur Rahman

DHAKA: Bangladesh foreign minister Khalilur Rahman Wednesday emphasised the need to address “some irritations” that exist in Bangladesh-India ties, noting govt is reviewing India’s invitation to PM Tarique Rahman for the Sept Brics Summit in New Delhi.Talking to reporters following a meeting with Indian high commissioner to Bangladesh Dinesh Trivedi, he said the neighbhours would move their bilateral relations forward on the basis of sovereign equality, with due consideration for their mutual interests. “We did not talk about any specific issue. There are some irritations. He knows it. I know it, too. It is very important to resolve them. Everyone understands that need,” Khalilur said, in an apparent reference to former PM Sheikh Hasina’s extradition and the alleged issue of “push-backs” on the border.Earlier, Bangladesh PM bypassed India to prioritise a state visit to China, despite an early invitation from PM Modi. The minister, however, said, “Regarding the resetting of relations between the two countries, we have said this before, and we both agree on this issue.”
Article Summary: Bangladesh foreign minister Khalilur Rahman emphasised the need to address “some irritations” that exist in Bangladesh-India ties. He said the neighbhours would move their bilateral relations forward on the basis of sovereign equality.

Article Title: Sri Lanka: Sri Lanka investigates Chinese triad angle in port city murder
Article Text: A violent gang war in Sri Lanka’s Colombo Port City has sparked a major criminal investigation, exposing potential links to a transnational cyber fraud network tied to Chinese organised crime syndicates.A Chinese national who was abducted and later found dead was identified as an individual allegedly connected to computer fraud activities, reported Sri Lanka’s News 1st. The incident has put the spotlight back on Chinese criminal networks active in the China-built port city, highlighting also the pitfalls of Chinese investment and development.According to local media reports, three Chinese nationals engaging in fishing on a port city suspension bridge were ambushed by around 20 Chinese men. The attackers threatened the victims with firearms, severely assaulted them, and abducted all three. Two victims were later discovered tied up inside an abandoned van within the city, while the third was taken away. Hours later, the third victim’s body was found blindfolded.Police revealed that the Chinese nationals involved were not lawfully employed in Sri Lanka. Following an investigation, said the News 1st report, officers attached to the Colombo Crimes Division intercepted two Chinese suspects at Bandaranaike International Airport as they allegedly attempted to board a flight to Singapore.Meanwhile, a special security operation has been launched by local authorities to ensure the safety of Chinese residents across Colombo, according to the news report.This case highlights a broader trend across Sri Lanka, where authorities have arrested numerous foreign nationals operating scam centres —including “pig butchering” investment schemes. Investigators suspect that recent international crackdowns across Dubai, Myanmar, Laos, and Cambodia have pushed elements of these Chinese Triad-linked crime networks into Sri Lanka, transforming the island nation into an emerging operational front for global cybercrime syndicates.
Article Summary: A Chinese national who was abducted and later found dead was identified as an individual allegedly connected to computer fraud activities. The incident has put the spotlight back on Chinese criminal networks active in the China-built port city, highlighting also the pitfalls of Chinese investment and development.

Article Title: 'Currently reviewing': Bangladesh on PM Modi's invitation to Tarique Rahman for India visit
Article Text:
Minister of Foreign Affairs Bangladesh (AP image)

India reiterates commitment to stronger ties

Dhaka flags 'irritants' in bilateral ties

Bangladesh foreign minister Khalilur Rahman on Wednesday said that Prime Minister Narendra Modi's invitation to Tarique Rahman to visit India for the upcoming 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi is under review currently.The remarks came after Indian High Commissioner Dinesh Trivedi paid a courtesy call on the minister, five weeks after taking charge as India's envoy to Bangladesh."We are currently reviewing it (the invitation)," Rahman told the reporters. He said the prime minister had received several invitations for foreign visits and was also scheduled to attend the UN General Assembly in New York."So, we have to consider all these engagements together," he added.Prime Minister Modi had first invited Rahman and his family to visit India in February. A fresh invitation to attend the BRICS Summit was sent last week, according to officials.The Indian High Commission in Dhaka said High Commissioner Trivedi reaffirmed India's commitment to a "positive, constructive and forward-looking partnership" with Bangladesh based on mutual interests and benefits, PTI cited.The High Commission also said Trivedi met state minister for foreign affairs Shama Obaed Islam for a wide-ranging discussion on strengthening bilateral cooperation across sectors. Speaking after the meeting, Trivedi said a visit by the Bangladeshi prime minister was entirely Dhaka's decision but added that India was "eagerly looking forward" to welcoming him."We hope the visit will take place very soon," he said.Rahman said both countries agreed that bilateral relations should move forward on the basis of mutual interests and sovereign equality. However, he acknowledged that certain "irritants" in the relationship needed to be addressed."He knows about them, and I know about them. It is very important that these irritants are addressed," the foreign minister said.Asked whether the issue of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina's extradition from India was discussed, Rahman said all bilateral issues would be taken up in future discussions.Hasina has been living in India since leaving Bangladesh following the collapse of her government in August 2024. Dhaka has repeatedly sought her extradition to face legal proceedings.
Article Summary: Bangladesh foreign minister Khalilur Rahman says invitation to visit India for BRICS Summit is under review. Indian High Commissioner Dinesh Trivedi paid a courtesy call on the minister, five weeks after taking charge as India's envoy to Bangladesh.

Article Title: Ousted PM Sheikh Hasina plans Bangladesh return: 'I may be killed, I may be sent to prison'
Article Text: Bangladesh's ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina on Wednesday said she was determined to return to her country by December despite facing the possibility of arrest, imprisonment or even execution.The 78-year-old former leader, who has been living in New Delhi since fleeing Bangladesh in August 2024, said she was prepared to face the consequences of returning home."I may be killed. I may be arrested. I may be sent to prison," Hasina said in an email response to questions by AFP."I am fully aware of my fate. Still, I want to go back because my people are calling me," she added.Earlier this month, Hasina had also told Reuters that she and her political allies would return from exile and face the courts in Bangladesh."My party leaders and workers are being subjected to tremendous repression," she had told Reuters. "If death comes, I want it to come on my own soil, where my parents are buried and where their blood was shed," she added.Hasina was sentenced to death in absentia by Bangladesh's International Crimes Tribunal over her government's handling of the 2024 student-led protests that ultimately ended her 15-year rule.The protests began as demonstrations against the country's government job quota system but quickly evolved into a nationwide anti-government movement after security forces launched a crackdown on protesters.Thousands were injured, while many were detained during the months-long protests.As the demonstrations intensified and spread across the country, Hasina resigned and fled in August 2024, ending her tenure as prime minister.Following the change in government, Bangladesh's International Crimes Tribunal initiated multiple cases against Hasina and several of her former ministers over allegations of crimes against humanity linked to the crackdown.Her Awami League has since been banned from political activities, while several senior party leaders have been arrested or are facing legal proceedings.Earlier this year, Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) chief Tarique Rahman was sworn in as the country's new prime minister. He became the first elected male premier after decades of politics dominated by Sheikh Hasina and his mother, former prime minister Khaleda Zia, a long-running rivalry often described as the "battle of the begums."
Article Summary: Sheikh Hasina has been living in New Delhi since fleeing Bangladesh in August 2024. She was sentenced to death in absentia by Bangladesh's International Crimes Tribunal over her government's handling of the 2024 student-led protests. The protests began as demonstrations against the country's government job quota system.
